carbon catabolites repress 3,4- dichloroaniline degradation in biofilms, and that cell dispersal affects 3,4 - dichloroanilin e degradation in biofilms.

the presence of an additional organic carbon source, citrate, affects the degradation of the organic pollutant 3,4-DCAn in biofilms of Comamonas testosteroni WDL7-RFPeven though the additional organic carbon source does not directly affect the degradation of the pollutant.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between carbon catabolism, cell physiology, biofilm structure, and pollutant degradation in biofilms.

understanding how biofilm structure, cell physiology and C substrate availability interact in pollutant degradation in biofilms and how this can be exploited for improved pollutant removal in engineered systems.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of citric acid as a carbon source leads to CCR, which in turn reduces the specific 3,CA degrading activity in the biofilm, which in turn leads to a higher 3,4-DC concentration in the bulk liquid, which in turn causes increased cell dispersal, which in turn results in a reduced biofilm biomass.
the availability of an additional C source to the biofilm will lead to CCR of the pollutant degrading enzyme(s) and increased cell dispersal, resulting in lower pollutant removal efficiencies.

the effect of CCR on pollutant degradation in biofilms is not as simple as in planktonic cultures and that the interplay between CCR, growth and cell dispersal in biofilms is complex and requires further study to be understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CCR in biofilms is a more complex phenomenon than in planktonic cells, as it is affected by changes in cell physiology and biofilm architecture.
the presence of auxiliary carbon sources may lead to CCR and/or increased cell dispersal that together may affect pollutant degradation in biofilms.

CCR in the presence of an auxiliary carbon source is not only a result of the presence of an alternative carbon source but also a result of the lower specific pollutant degradation activity and increased pollutant exposure in the presence of the alternative carbon source.
The main takeaway from our work is that
biofilm systems are not as robust as previously thought and that they can easily be affected by changes in the surrounding environment.
the effects of auxiliary organic C sources on pollutant removal from biofilms cannot be predicted solely based on growth on the auxiliary C source.

the effects of auxiliary C source availability on pollutant degradation in biofilms are complex and that the effect on pollutant degradation rates cannot be predicted from the growth rates on the auxiliary C source.
